title: When is the right time to be innovative during an emergency? (a personal experience)
html:
A couple months ago, I was riding my motorcycle to the office just as I have so many other days in the past. Nothing was different. Until it wasn’t. In a split second I was avoiding a collision, slamming on my brakes and tipping hard to the left. I must have blacked out for a moment as the next thing that I remember is a friendly bystander speaking calmly to me as I tried to sit up on the road. I was in a lot of pain, but he kept reassuring me that things were going to be okay. I was in shock. Meanwhile, a second bystander had moved my motorcycle and called the emergency services. These bystanders were my first responders.

Within what felt like moments, the ambulance had arrived and the paramedics had braced my neck, completed preliminary checks, did more thorough checks related to my specific pain points and confirmed my general awareness (i.e. no concussion). By the time I was in the ambulance, the police had arrived, took my statement, conducted a breathalyzer, and took my contact details. On the way to the hospital, the paramedics administered pain control medication and examined my injuries in much greater detail.

Interesting enough, what I remember the most about the journey to the hospital was the ad hoc conversation a paramedic and I had in the ambulance about Canada (my home country) – not specifically because of the content, but because this was the time when the paramedic was adapting, attempting to make my experience less dreadful by some way of distraction.

Upon arriving at the hospital, there was no delay. I was wheeled directly to a room and the paramedics did a succinct hand-over with the doctor and nurses. Procedures were followed, duplication was avoided, and information was managed.

Upon reflection, I recognized that it was a time when I was depending on the system to work. I did not want the emergency responders experimenting or innovating when I was in urgent need. They customized and adapted, but it was not in a way that I lost any confidence.

While I know that my minor accident is, in no way, comparable to the large, complex humanitarian crises to which I often respond, it did give me a small, closed situation to study. It got me thinking: when is it appropriate to be innovative during a humanitarian crisis?

Perhaps we could break down an emergency by response type to determine where, in its timeline, new ideas or approaches would be appropriate. As the analogy of the motorcycle accident can attest, hands-on life-saving activities must work from the very beginning. Victims are depending on it. But, as I have outlined before, crises also introduce situations that enable or call for innovative approaches.

In the past month, I have had similar discussions with first responders in Nepal. With all the talk and push on humanitarian innovation over the past couple years, these responders struggled to balance their regular, required work (in which they were trained) and the seemingly constant external pressure to do something new.

So, where are the ideal points for the introduction of innovation? When should it be pushed and when should it get out of the way? Perhaps how we support the first responders remotely in the early days could always be innovating while pushing for innovative approaches in-country after a few weeks? Figuring out such a framework may also help to break-down the humanitarian decision maker challenge we continue to face.

I don’t have the answers. It feels more like an idea in formulation and the start of a conversation.

Andrej
teaser: After a motorcycle accident, reflections on how paramedics and hospital staff adapted and followed procedure, and on when innovation fits an emergency. An idea in formulation.
seo_description: A personal story of an accident and what it suggests about when it is right to be innovative during an emergency response.
